entries.title: DMV High School Football Players of Week 2
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts included a bruising back from Gonzaga and a ball hawk from C.G. Woodson.
entries.content:
With Maryland public schools kicking off this past weekend, high school football season is officially in full swing in the D.C. area. Here’s who made their mark in Week 2:

David Anderson, senior, quarterback, Theodore Roosevelt

With Anderson under center, the Roughriders’ offense exploded in a season-opening 40-15 victory over KIPP. The senior torched the Bulldogs, passing for 252 passing and three touchdowns. He also added a fourth score on the ground as Roosevelt kicked off a new year with a statement victory. Anderson’s connection with senior wide receiver Gabe Hudgens could make for one of the strongest combinations in the city as coach Chris Harden’s team looks to bounce back from last year’s dramatic playoff loss to Dunbar.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Asheton Burton, senior, running back, Gonzaga

After a slew of early turnovers Thursday against Coolidge, Gonzaga’s offense needed a spark. With the game still scoreless midway through the second quarter, the Eagles handed the ball to Burton, the team’s bruising running back, nine straight times and the senior marched his team down the field. Burton scored from 2 yards out for the game’s first points, then pulled off a second-half hat trick with three more touchdown runs as Gonzaga rolled to a 33-0 victory. Burton’s final touchdown run of the night was arguably his most impressive as he bulldozed his way through a horde of Coolidge defenders for a 14-yard score.

Corey Smith Jr., junior, wide receiver, Good Counsel

The Falcons earned their first win of the Sal Gorgone era in thrilling fashion Friday, turning New Jersey powerhouse Bergen Catholic away at the goal line in the closing seconds of the game to seal a 41-39 win. Smith, a towering 6-foot-5, 210-pound receiver whose Division I offer list includes Maryland and Virginia Tech, caught three touchdowns and racked up 131 receiving yards. “What a beautiful athlete,” Gorgone said of Smith after the win. “He’s a playmaker, and he makes those plays in clutch moments.”

Darren Theobald, senior, defensive back, C.G. Woodson

Theobald pulled down three interceptions for the Cavaliers in Thursday’s 28-7 victory over Edison. The first came on the game’s opening drive, when the senior grabbed an Eagles pass in the corner of the end zone to squash Edison’s momentum. The second came with the game knotted at 7 in the third quarter, and it was followed by a long Woodson touchdown drive. Theobald’s busy night peaked in the fourth quarter when he hauled in a 33-yard receiving touchdown at wide receiver before switching to defense and snatching a third pick to clinch a victory. Theobald and the Cavaliers will look to replicate their defensive performance next week against Oakton, whose high-powered offense is averaging 49 points per game.

Jamie White Jr., senior, defensive back, Quince Orchard

It didn’t take long for White, a senior transfer from St. Frances, to make an impact with the Cougars. In his first game, the defensive back nabbed an interception on the first play from scrimmage. It would be his first of three on the night. The Cougars, two-time defending Maryland 4A champions, earned their 28th straight victory with a 28-0 win over Paint Branch. With White and three-star senior Rico Jackson patrolling the secondary and senior Pittsburgh commit Jaheim Bond wreaking havoc up front, coach John Kelley’s defense is again among the area’s best.

To nominate a local player for next week’s roundup, send us an email with their name and stats. See last week’s selections here.

entries.title: Self-Funders Are Still Terrible at Getting Themselves Elected
entries.summary: Ultrarich politicians — in most cases — can’t buy a seat in Congress.
entries.content:
It’s still exceedingly difficult to buy oneself a seat in Congress.

During the 2026 midterms, a record number of wealthy Americans — 69 — have spent more than $1 million of their own money to support their campaigns for federal office.

And with primary season ending in the next several days with contests in New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Delaware, about two-thirds of these self-funding candidates have turned out to be losers who couldn’t advance to the November general election.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ub0ox/4/Those who bet big on themselves to win their races for Congress collectively loaned their campaigns $160 million.

At the extreme, former Rep. David Trone burned through about $25 million of his own cash only to lose in his Maryland 6th Congressional District primary by 7 percentage points to fellow Democratic Rep. April McClain Delaney.
David.Trone.1 (5515x3677, AR: 1.50)In Arizona, businessman Daniel Keenan spent $1.6 million on his failed bid to replace Republican Rep. Andy Biggs.

Keenan says the run was well worth it even if he lost the Republican primary to former county sheriff Mark Lamb in July.

“I did it to contribute to my country, to do the best I can to make my country better off for my kids,” he said. “It was never for personal gain or ego or anything like that.”

Keenan also expects to one day run again: “I worked my butt off … went from polling at 1% to capturing nearly 42% of the vote. I think we ran a really good campaign and set myself up well for future runs.”

Still, Keenan said he was surprised by “the amount of prominent Republicans who privately reached out to me and supported me” but wouldn’t do so publicly.

“I was the most Trump-aligned candidate and again defending all those policies at every chance I could, and it was difficult not getting the support from the White House,” he said.

On the other end of that spectrum is Thomas Chalifoux, a retired Army colonel and businessman who sought the Republican nomination in Florida’s 9th Congressional District.

Chalifoux placed third in the Republican primary, having spent upward of $2 million on his ultimately failed campaign. It was a worse showing than his 2024 bid for the same seat, which saw him secure the GOP nomination but lose in the general election to Democratic Rep. Darren Soto.

That race also cost him upward of $2 million — a fraction of his net worth, which sits at around $270 million, per his most recent federal financial disclosure. Still, he is quick to point out: “I started with nothing, just like Elon Musk.”

Chalifoux previously taught military strategy at the Army Command and General Staff College and, more than anything, seemed disappointed he would not have the chance to go against the “bunch of rubber stamps in Congress” who have supported President Donald Trump’s war with Iran.

“The Iran ‘Epic Fury’ is just poorly, poorly planned. We've got a mess on our hands, and it makes American military power look much worse,” Chalifoux said. Trump “created a climate where no one wants to disagree because he's very vindictive.”Might he try a third time come 2028?

“I don't know. I'm 78 … people look at that as being too old. I'm not too old,” he said, noting he is a “world-class bodybuilder” whose mother “is over 100, so I've got that longevity in my family.”

Earlier this year, Keith Gross and John Fleming, candidates for Florida’s 2nd Congressional District and U.S. Senate in Louisiana, respectively, each spent around $12 million on their failed primary campaigns.
John.Fleming (7023x4682, AR: 1.50)Democrat Peter Chatzky entered, then exited, the race for New York's 17th Congressional District after the resurfacing of lewd social media posts in March. He ultimately recouped $10.7 million of the $11.3 million he had loaned his campaign, according to Federal Election Commission records.

The number of self-funders who ultimately lost their elections is expected to grow in November.

Don Tracy and Barb Regnitz, the Republican nominees for U.S. Senate in Illinois and Indiana’s 1st Congressional District, respectively, each put in upward of $2 million into their campaigns so far. But both are vying for “solid” or “likely” Democratic seats and are expected to lose.

entries.title: A Big Dig
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Sept. 8, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

When a century-old D.C. library is standing on nothing but stilts, it can make anyone nervous.

“One wrong move by one excavator could take the whole thing down, so the stakes were literally very high,” says Jaspreet Pahwa, the director of capital planning and construction for the D.C. Public Library system.

That was one of the pitfalls of the 2 ½-year renovation of the Southeast Library in Eastern Market, which wraps up this week ahead of the library’s reopening on Thursday.

It was built in 1922 as one of the city’s three Carnegie libraries — the others are in Takoma and Mount Pleasant — so library officials had to balance protecting the historical landmark with trying to expand one of the 10 busiest neighborhood libraries in the city.

That involved digging between 24 and 40 feet under and around the building, allowing for an expansion of the ground-floor level and the addition of a basement level that will now largely serve kids. With that, the Southeast Library will double in size but leave the original historic building largely intact.

“This was a really complex project, to say the least,” says Rich Reyes-Gavilan, DCPL’s executive director. “The need was there. It was just about finding the money and the ingenuity and the know-how.”

To ensure the new basement level didn’t feel like it’s underground, a new skylight was carved from the roof down the center of the building, drawing natural light all the way into the deepest recesses of the library. Reyes-Gavilan — who has overseen the modernization of dozens of libraries in his 13 years leading DCPL — says the skylight is the library’s “architectural marvel."

And there’s more: An extension was built in what used to be an alley behind the library, connecting it to a neighboring rowhouse and allowing for a new main entrance to be constructed along South Carolina Avenue.

The renovation wasn’t cheap. The $40 million price tag is roughly double what was originally contemplated, because of both increasing construction costs and a need to comply with historic preservation rules. But library officials say they were able to leverage federal COVID recovery funds to pay for it.

The next projects for the library system include a brand-new facility in Congress Heights and another in Eckington/Edgewood. Future renovations include libraries in Chevy Chase and Shepherd Park. To Reyes-Gavilan’s relief, none of these projects is expected to be as complicated as the Southeast Library makeover.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A federal planning commission has approved the transfer of the D.C. Armory, the headquarters of the District’s National Guard, to local control, NOTUS’ Kendall Staton reports. The transfer still has to be approved by D.C.’s mayor, the D.C. Council and Congress.

D.C.’s Department of Public Works is testing rat-proof trash bins in high-traffic areas of the city, WUSA9 reports.

President Donald Trump has become obsessed with “architectural immortality” — building monuments around D.C. that will outlast him, New York Magazine reports.

Former Kennedy Center chair David Rubenstein has purchased the large sculpture that was removed from the grounds of the venue last week, The New York Times reports. Rubenstein, a billionaire philanthropist who owns the Orioles, sat as chair from 2010 to 2025, when he was ousted as part of Trump’s takeover of the center’s board. Rubenstein reportedly paid more than $2 million for the abstract sculpture, titled “Blue.”

The grieving tree: D.C. residents have been leaving condolence messages on a large tree in Dupont Circle that was severed by last week’s wild storm.





FROM MARYLAND

All aboard! The stretch of the Red Line between North Bethesda and Friendship Heights reopened Monday after nine weeks of construction work. The project finished “on time and on budget,” Metro said in a news release.





D.C. TRIVIA


Where did the first D.C. Public Library branch open in 1911?

  1. Anacostia
  2. Capitol Hill
  3. Takoma
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Jayden Daniels camp AP - 26238573512493 (3872x2581, AR: 1.50)
The Commanders should have plenty of bulletin board material this season. In a roundup of preseason coverage and power rankings, NOTUS’ Alex Schiffer reports that many national analysts and pundits are down on Washington ahead of a pivotal year for GM Adam Peters and coach Dan Quinn.

“Skinny quarterback who got hurt last year combined with nobody who can block?” The Ringer’s Bill Simmons said on a recent podcast. “I’m out.”

High school football season is fully underway, with Maryland public schools kicking off this past weekend. NOTUS’ Noah Ferguson highlights five standouts from around the area in our Players of the Week column; this week’s group includes a Quince Orchard DB who nabbed three interceptions and a Gonzaga running back who scored four touchdowns.

DMV native Frances Tiafoe has advanced to the quarterfinals of the U.S. Open. The 28-year-old Tiafoe, currently ranked the No. 12 men’s tennis player in the world, will face 22-year-old American Alex Michelsen today at 1 p.m. Tiafoe is chasing his first Grand Slam title.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Padres, 9:40 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Library photo courtesy of the D.C. Public Library system. Commanders photo by Stephanie Scarbrough/AP.

entries.title: Down in Dallas
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What’s the message out of Republicans’ midterm convention? Nearly 70 candidates have self-funded their campaigns; most lost. Democrats eye a DOGE-ish idea. And: What's happening with the screwworm scare?

THE LATEST

There's been a lot of reporting about Republicans frustrated with White House messaging — that it’s all about Donald Trump, and not about what voters care about, or at least what to tell them 56 days from the midterms. This week in Dallas, the party’s midterm convention could provide another taste of that messaging.

If last month is any preview, expect to hear about communism, liberals and how Democrats, including Joe Biden, are to blame for the current ills. Nearly 20 months into office, Trump still often mentions the former president — dropping more than a dozen references to Biden in August alone.

A White House official told NOTUS that Trump has made Biden his foil because “he’s drawing a contrast with the historic successes of his first 19 months with the Biden years.”

Former Biden White House comms strategist Andrew Bates — who’s advising multiple Democratic campaigns this cycle — says he thinks Trump’s references to his predecessor only underscore how good things were pre-Trump. Republicans “going out of their way to bring up a time when the economy was stronger and we weren’t stuck in Iran just highlights how much they’ve ripped off the American people and failed the tests they set for themselves in 2024,” he said.

Trump launched a torrent of Truth Social posts this weekend: sharing fake AI images of “Iran's Navy” on the ocean floor; claiming the moon and the Strait of Hormuz as American territory; depicting Mexico, Canada and Greenland covered in the red, white and blue; rebranding New Mexico as “New America.”

He also celebrated shiny D.C. statues and fountains, unveiled Space Force uniforms and brought George Washington to the Oval Office for a chitchat. And, of course, he posted Biden wearing a Trump 2024 cap. Those issues aren’t necessarily topping voters’ lists — It may cost me $100 to fill up my truck but dammit, have we renamed New Mexico? It could explain why so many Republicans didn’t buy a ticket to Texas.

More on NOTUS: Suspect Identified in Attack on Ohio Gubernatorial Candidate Amy Acton | Missouri Group Asks the Supreme Court to Let Former District Maps Stand | German Far-Right Party Is Projected to Win Regional Election | Trump Administration Asks the Supreme Court to Lift Block on Mail-in Voting Regulations


From the campaign trail


Self-funding and still coming up short. A record number of wealthy candidates — 69 — have so far spent more than $1 million of their own money to support their campaigns for federal office, NOTUS’ Mark Alfred reports. And as primary season ends, about two-thirds of these self-funders have already turned out to be losers. Mark spoke with some of them, and a surprisingly high number said the experience of spending millions of their own dollars just to flame out has left them hungry to run again.

From a potential future 


Democrats wanna DOGE, too. The Trump team and DOGE were “correct in identifying that people want things to work better,” Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger told NOTUS’ Natalie Alms. “Rather cynically, they used that sentiment to their electoral advantage, and then used it as a mandate to break things further.” She’s one of many Democrats who say there's a way to pick up the mantle Elon Musk nominally claimed — tech modernization — to showcase that liberals can make state and local governments hum. Natalie explores how some in the Democratic Party hope they’ll get the chance to unleash their own DOGE soon.


NOTUS METRO

Local news: D.C. Is on Track to Control Armory Land Near RFK Stadium, by Kendall Staton

Sports desk: National Pundits Have Low Expectations for the Commanders This Season, by Alex Schiffer

DMV High School Football Players of Week 2, by Noah Ferguson

NEW ON NOTUS

The strange case of the disappearing screwworm. The dangerous pest, discovered within the United States in June, has been targeted by the Agriculture Department with the goal of protecting cattle and other livestock herds from an infestation straight out of a horror movie. The effort was expected to take years, NOTUS’ Tyler Spence writes, but in August the USDA publicly reported that only four cases were detected, and none in cattle. Tyler writes that many people who follow the screwworm are very skeptical of this figure. “It doesn’t make a lot of sense, biologically,” a former longtime USDA official told NOTUS.

Some experts question whether the agency has the personnel and the resources to properly track and contain the screwworm, Tyler writes, and point to the significant department staff reductions from DOGE. The USDA says it’s simply very good at its job: “The low case count is a direct result of the aggressive, science-driven five-prong strategy to eradicate NWS unveiled by Secretary [Brooke] Rollins a year ago,” a spokesperson said.

More: Judge Says Trump Administration Must Provide 48 Hours’ Notice Before Arch Construction | Fetterman Dismisses Bombshell Report as ‘Smears’ and ‘Half-Truths’ | Trump’s Super PAC Drops $10 Million in Texas Senate Race

NOT US

  • For Fired DeSantis Campaign Staff Member, a Second Chance at State Dept., by Andrea Fuller, Ken Bensinger and Edward Wong for The New York Times
  • The DSA Is Using Coffee With Comrades and Socialist Softball to Convert the Curious, by Joshua Chaffin and Maya Davis for The Wall Street Journal
  • Hot-Dog Heaven: Inside Trump’s Golf Getaways, by Dan Alexander for Forbes
  • A CNN journalist spent years reporting on al-Qaeda. Now he’s handing over a massive archive. By Scott Nover for The Washington Post

WEEK AHEAD

Today

Primary election in New Hampshire.

Trump delivers remarks at Steel Across America.

Wednesday

The Republican midterm convention begins in Dallas.

Primary election in Rhode Island.

Thursday

Trump headlines the Republican midterm convention.

One year since the assassination of Charlie Kirk in Utah.

Friday

25 years since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Monthly Consumer Price Index numbers released.

Saturday

Trump travels to Ireland.


Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com.

entries.title: National Pundits Have Low Expectations for the Commanders This Season
entries.summary: Ahead of a pivotal year, coach Dan Quinn’s team has not received a lot of love from analysts.
entries.content:
The Commanders open a third season under coach Dan Quinn on Sunday with an afternoon matchup against the Eagles.

After a dream campaign in 2024, last year did not go to plan for Washington and the team finished 5-12. Projections for this year are wide-ranging, with a few analysts hopeful for the Commanders but many expecting a long season.

What They’re Saying

The Ringer’s Bill Simmons said on a recent podcast that the Commanders are a “lock” to finish under the 7.5 wins FanDuel has projected for the team.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“They lost [Laremy] Tunsil for the season and I didn’t like their offensive line to begin with,” Simmons said. “If you’re reading the day-to-day reports, really rough stuff with the offensive line. Which, normally not everybody has a good offensive line — but their quarterback is 127 pounds. So the skinny quarterback who got hurt last year combined with nobody who can block? I’m out.”

ESPN analyst and former NFL quarterback Dan Orlovsky named the Commanders the league’s most confusing team in an interview with Dan Patrick on Friday. Orlovsky cited the Commanders’ busy offseason and 31-year-old David Blough as a first-time offensive coordinator among his concerns with the organization.

“What’s the offensive actually going to be?” Orlovsky said. “You lose your left tackle who you just made the highest-paid left tackle in football and all your fans are like, ‘We'll be OK.’ Those two things can't happen at the same time. … It's an unbelievably expensive defense but a little bit unproven. …”

“And so it could go really good if they gel and those high-end-paid players play at such a high level and the free agent signings and the draft picks play at such a high level. Or it could be a season of question, of, ‘OK where is this organization headed,’ and a second year of maybe some up and down from Jayden Daniels. I’m bullish on them, but I’m just not all in.”

Power Rankings 

Yahoo! Sports has the Commanders in its “work to do” category, citing player development and injury luck as two factors that could define the season.

Similarly, CBS Sports ranked the team in the C tier of its power rankings, which is for teams that could make the playoffs if everything goes right.

ESPN has the Commanders 20th in its power rankings, one spot lower than where the network ranked the team after last spring’s draft.

The Athletic recently ranked the Commanders 13th of the 16 teams in its NFC power ranking and put Washington 23rd in its league ranking before training camp. The NFC ranking was conducted with multiple team executives weighing in. One executive told The Athletic that a healthy Daniels is enough to make up for the numerous question marks surrounding the team.

"They get Jayden back, and Terry McLaurin will be healthy," the executive told The Athletic. "They've added some really good parts defensively in free agency. They have to get the offensive line solidified."

Another executive was much less optimistic.

"I think they are going to be bad," they said. "The quarterback is talented, but his style of play, unless he changes it, is a concern. The weapons around him are OK, but I don't think it's a dynamic team offensively. Defensively, they plateaued."

Long odds

The sportsbooks have a similar take, giving Washington long odds to make a real impact this season. On Monday at FanDuel, the Commanders were (+265) to make the playoffs, (+550) to win the division and (+6500) to win the Super Bowl. The odds at DraftKings are similar. Essentially, the books think the Commanders have less than a 30% chance to make the playoffs.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: Democrats Are Plotting Government Efficiency in a Post-DOGE World
entries.summary: Rising stars in the Democratic Party are promoting their tech modernization teams in a post-DOGE political landscape.
entries.content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made a big show of bringing his “pothole politics” online: He donned his sunglasses, lowered himself into a go-kart and took a lap around a track in Coney Island to sell his new Public Interest Technology Crew, or PIT Crew. (Get it?)

The team’s mission is to make the city’s clunky online systems easier to use and to help enact his agenda. It’s an initiative Democrats are adopting across the country. In Virginia, Gov. Abigail Spanberger, too, is setting up a crew of tech whizzes to bring government services into the 21st century.

Many of the people running those teams are alumni of the U.S. Digital Service, the relatively unknown Obama-era tech squad that President Donald Trump transformed into DOGE on Day 1 of his second administration.

Now, they’re out of Washington and working for some of the rising stars of the Democratic Party who want to use technology to enact the liberal agenda and show voters that they can get things done.

“What I heard along the campaign trail, and certainly now that I’ve been governor, is people have this sense that things don’t work,” Spanberger told NOTUS in an interview.

The Trump team and DOGE were “correct in identifying that people want things to work better,” she said. “Rather cynically, they used that sentiment to their electoral advantage, and then used it as a mandate to break things further.”

More than 10 blue states have digital services teams — many of them with former U.S. Digital Service staffers and several of them established before the second Trump administration. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro set up a digital team in 2023. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, in 2024. By comparison, only two red states have similar units.

The teams are an answer to what Donald Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, calls a progressive “neuroses” that wants to prove liberals can govern effectively, part of a movement calling for “abundance” — more development, more ambitious policies, faster.

That, and the national focus on DOGE, have brought what was once a relatively behind-the-scenes administrative effort, like building a website, into the foreground.

“Doing the good work is the core of what we need to do every day,” said Luke Farrell, a deputy commissioner and senior adviser for the New York City government. “But also, we then need to show people the work, and we need to get it into people’s hands.”

Mamdani’s PIT Crew has been tasked with making his administration’s “click-to-cancel” rule into a reality with an online portal for New Yorkers to file complaints. The consumer protection rule, which requires businesses to provide simple subscription cancellation, is projected to save New Yorkers millions of dollars once it goes into effect next month.

In Virginia, the digital team is being told to address the inefficiencies that disrupt the daily lives of residents; Virginians still have to write checks to the state because they can’t pay for some state services online, Spanberger said. Other parts of the state government still require traditional signatures.

“One of the ways that you can best ensure that you're correctly utilizing state taxpayer dollars is to make things actually work,” Spanberger said. “The state digital service is meant to be a part of that.”
Abigail Spanberger AP-23311573084272 (4411x2941, AR: 1.50)President Barack Obama set up the U.S. Digital Service in 2014 to fix HealthCare.gov after a botched rollout threatened to tank Obamacare, one of the Obama administration’s signature policies. The unit became a core part of a network of tech do-gooders in the federal government.

After the HealthCare.gov rescue, the team largely operated in the background of government. During the first Trump administration, the leadership of the U.S. Digital Service fashioned the team as a nonpartisan unit. In a shift, the Biden administration installed political leadership and tasked it with working on priorities like building a government program to file federal taxes for free.

Still, when Trump returned to office, few Americans were familiar with the tech team that the president and Elon Musk transformed into DOGE.

In the early months of the second Trump administration, many of the existing U.S. Digital Service staffers were laid off. Others resigned publicly, saying that DOGE’s work was antithetical to the mission of the original team. 18F, another Obama-era government tech team, was shuttered in March 2025, weeks after Musk tweeted that it had been “deleted.”

DOGE quickly departed from its nominal tech focus to overhaul of the federal workforce and slash government spending — moves that inspired nationwide protests and lawsuits. The backlash has given Democrats nationally an opportunity to reclaim the government efficiency mantle.

That conversation has already begun in Washington. Liberal think tanks and former federal officials are drafting plans for how future administrations could improve the government, as NOTUS has previously reported. The work could have an impact beyond political resonance: In New York, Virginia and the capital alike, these efforts to improve technology and government could help politicians actually implement their agendas.

“A policy without a way to enforce it isn’t really a policy at all,” Erie Meyer, who was previously the chief technologist at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, told NOTUS of the importance of the PIT Crew’s work implementing Mamdani’s click-to-cancel rule.

Mamdani’s team is still deciding on what other projects they’ll focus on, but the work will be “core to the Mamdani administration's agenda around affordability, housing, consumer and worker protection and more,” said Maya Israni, senior adviser to the city’s chief technology officer.

More than 4,000 people have submitted applications to join the New York City PIT crews, which will consist of five teams focusing on building services in-house instead of using contractors.

“We really want to have a direct impact on someone’s day-to-day life as a New Yorker and make their life on a day-to-day basis better and more affordable,” Israni said. “We’re here to deliver on core Mamdani administration priorities.”

At the state level, Democrats are also using the teams to respond to Trump’s agenda. Spanberger said Virginia’s tech push is especially relevant in light of the Republican budget law passed last year, which slashed federal funding in food assistance programs and Medicaid.

As the state implements Medicaid work requirements from that law, how well various state systems interface to validate eligibility becomes really important, said Spanberger, noting that “any of those gaps means loss of coverage or means loss of social safety net programs for people in a way that can really be harmful.”

The tension: Sometimes the work to enable policies isn’t flashy.

The goal of the new tech unit in Virginia is to “improve the services that the government provides for every Virginian,” Andrea Fletcher — who also previously worked in the U.S. Digital Service and just recently started as the new director of the Virginia Digital Service — told NOTUS.

To do that, the Virginia team will also be looking to tackle the “boring stuff” that often makes the government headache-inducing in the first place, like procurement and hiring, she said.

During DOGE’s heyday in Washington, some who had previously been on civic tech teams in Washington expressed envy at the political aircover Elon Musk’s team had to get things done.

The teams in New York and Virginia have that top-down investment, said Lynn Overmann, who worked as a senior adviser for the Biden administration as part of the U.S. Digital Service.

The real test, she said: “Can they actually get it done?”
entries.author: Natalie Alms

entries.title: Screwworm Cases Are Going Down. Experts Are Suspicious.
entries.summary: “It doesn’t make a lot of sense, biologically,” a former longtime USDA official said.
entries.content:
America’s fight against the New World screwworm was expected to be a multiyear effort, yet the number of new cases has dropped to a surprisingly low level.

Only four cases of screwworm were detected in the U.S. in August and none of them in cattle, according to a dashboard maintained by the Agriculture Department. In June, there had been 30 cases detected, and an expectation that the fight against the screwworm had a long way to go.

That August number baffles experts, given how far the screwworm had advanced into Texas and the high number of cases in Mexico and Central America.

“It’s very strange,” a former longtime USDA official who worked for the department’s plant and animal health department told NOTUS. “It doesn’t make a lot of sense, biologically.”

On top of that, the USDA reports it hasn’t detected screwworm through trapping flies or seeing the pest in any wildlife or feral animals, the primary ways officials might expect to keep tabs on the population and their movement.

“Zero cases in wildlife is unexplainable to me,” Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller told NOTUS. Miller said that he and horticulturists on his team have caught what they believed to be screwworm in traps, only to have the tests come back negative when sent to the USDA.

One current employee at the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service called the lack of cases in traps or wildlife “suspicious,” saying, “It doesn’t seem very likely to me that we haven’t trapped a single wild fly.”

The USDA says its playbook for fighting screwworm is working, which is why cases are so low. The New World screwworm is a fly that feeds on living tissue in animals and even humans. The infestation can be lethal to animals if left untreated and is considered a major threat to livestock in warm climates.

“The low case count is a direct result of the aggressive, science-driven five-prong strategy to eradicate NWS unveiled by Secretary [Brooke] Rollins a year ago,” a spokesperson for the USDA said in a statement. “This strategy, led by USDA and other federal partners, has increased tracking of the fly’s movement, inspections of impacted animals both wild and domestic, and substantially built up sterile fly capability through coordination with states and industry.”

The agency reopened the port of Douglas, Arizona, to livestock after more than a year of movement restrictions aimed at keeping the screwworm out of the U.S. The USDA conducts inspections of the livestock at the border and said it plans to reopen additional ports if successful in Douglas.

The agency also lifted movement restrictions on three counties this week ,two in Texas and one in New Mexico.

The USDA said on X that it has released 1 billion sterile flies, or male flies that mate with females but don’t produce offspring and effectively stop the lifecycle over time. Rollins and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote an op-ed Friday touting their efforts.

At the beginning of the summer, Rollins acknowledged that the agency needed 400 million more sterile flies a week to effectively combat the screwworm, a number that would likely take several months or a year to reach.

In the meantime, cases across Mexico and Central America have reached over 200,000, with 500 human cases in Mexico alone.

Some experts question whether the agency has the personnel and the resources to properly track and contain the screwworm. The USDA has undergone significant staffing reductions to many of its departments since the start of the second Trump administration.

“The critical mass is just not there to do the work that needs to be done,” the former USDA manager said.

And some former USDA officials question whether the current surveillance methods are working or whether screwworm is truly being contained effectively. “They're using wildlife cameras to do surveillance, and USDA is claiming that it works well, but it's also not catching anything,” a former USDA official who oversaw screwworm response told NOTUS.

Miller also raised doubts over the ability for cameras to identify open wounds and screwworm on animals, saying he has seen the video the cameras produce himself. “It’s not the best videos,” Miller said. He said the videos are fine for identifying animals, but are not the same as a medical examination.

The USDA said that the footage from these cameras is reviewed by wildlife biologists, with assistance from AI tools to identify animals with wounds.

Experts are also concerned that the current system does not incentivize ranchers to report cases. Current rules require cattle ranchers to keep their herds in quarantined areas, which can cause ranchers to lose money without any indemnity in return from the USDA.

Both former USDA officials said the USDA set up an indemnity program during the bird flu outbreaks beginning in 2024, something that has not been done for cattle ranchers with screwworm.

Both the current and former APHIS employees echoed this concern, saying ranchers would be uninterested in self-reporting due to concerns over movement restrictions or government surveillance.

The USDA said the agency provides indemnity for any animal that must be culled to prevent the spread of disease or parasites.

The U.S. eradication campaign that eventually beat back screwworm in the 20th century took the better part of a decade of sustained effort. USDA formally launched its sterile insect technique program across the southeastern U.S. in 1957. Florida was declared screwworm-free by 1958, and a large-scale push into Texas began in 1962, with ranchers reporting screwworm-free herds for the first time in modern memory by 1963. The U.S. wasn't declared fully free of the pest until 1966 — nine years after the campaign began in earnest.

Even then, the win proved fragile, with a resurgence tied to reinfestation from Mexico in 1972. Even after the 1966 declaration, eradication pushed steadily south over the following decades, with Mexico declared screwworm-free in 1991 and Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador following through the mid-1990s.

“I think it's still too early to tell what the situation is with the flies,” the current APHIS employee said before expressing optimism that screwworm has been defeated once and can be defeated again; it’s “just a matter of how much time and money it will take.”
